2 Two masses on a line: the balance point

html:
The big picture

A car has mass everywhere, but for many questions it behaves as if all its mass sat at one point, the center of mass (COM), with its whole weight \vec F_G acting there. For two masses on a massless beam, the COM is the balance point: there the turning effects of the two weights cancel (the lever rule), which makes the COM the mass-weighted average of the positions, x_c = (x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2)/(m_1 + m_2). More masses add more terms (discrete notation), separately for x, y and z. A real body is cut into infinitely many tiny pieces \mathrm dm, and the sum becomes an integral (continuous notation). If the density \rho is constant, \mathrm dm = \rho\,\mathrm dV and \rho cancels: the COM then depends only on the shape, and for a symmetric body like a cuboid it is the geometric center. Knowing the COM justifies the mass point model that kinematics uses from now on.

1 What the center of mass is

Lecture: board p. 4 (top) · Giancoli §9-8

Board sketches (p. 4). Top: a car with its weight \vec F_G drawn at one point → the car replaced by a single small circle carrying \vec F_G. Below (the "1D problem"): masses m_1 and m_2 on an x-axis, joined by a beam marked m = 0, held up by a finger between them; their weights \vec F_{G_1}, \vec F_{G_2} point down; x = 0 marks the origin.

Gravity pulls on every bit of a body. The claim of the top sketch is that, for the motion of the body as a whole, all those little pulls can be replaced by one force, the total weight \vec F_G, acting at one point. That point is the center of mass (COM).

Why one point is enough: the motion of any body, however it tumbles or turns, can be split into the motion of this one point plus a rotation (or wobble) about it. A thrown hammer spins wildly, yet its COM flies on a clean parabola, exactly like a thrown stone (6 Projectile Motion). For the path of the body as a whole, only the COM counts.

A diver tumbling through the air: her body turns in a complicated way, but one point, the center of mass (black dot), follows a clean parabola, just like a thrown ball. (Giancoli Fig. 9-21b)

The point where the total weight can be taken to act is strictly called the center of gravity. It coincides with the center of mass as long as \vec g is the same over the whole body, which holds for anything smaller than a mountain; the lecture uses the two interchangeably. It finds the point in three stages: two point masses on a line, many point masses in space, and a solid body.

The weight of a body of mass m (from 1 Physical Quantities and the SI System; properly in 8 Newton's Laws and Forces) is

\vec F_G = m \cdot \vec g, \qquad F_{G_1} = m_1 \cdot g, \qquad F_{G_2} = m_2 \cdot g
Symbols
  • \vec F_G — weight (gravitational force) of a body (N), pointing down; F_{G_1}, F_{G_2} — sizes of the weights of mass 1 and mass 2 (N)
  • m, m_1, m_2 — masses (kg)
  • \vec g — gravitational acceleration, pointing down; g = \lvert\vec g\rvert \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}

2 Two masses on a line: the balance point

Lecture: board p. 4 (bottom) – p. 5 (top) · Giancoli §9-8

The set-up (the "1D problem"): two point masses at the positions x_1 and x_2 on the x-axis, connected by a beam whose own mass is neglected ("m = 0"), so only the two weights count. A finger holds the beam up from below. Where must the finger be so that the beam stays level? That point is the COM, at position x_c.

Two expectations before calculating (board, with your notes):

  • Assumption m_2 > m_1: the balance point lies closer to m_2.
  • m_1 = m_2: it lies in the middle.

Two point masses on a line: the center of mass x_\text{CM} lies between them, closer to the heavier one. The book writes m_A, m_B for the lecture's m_1, m_2 and x_\text{CM} for x_c. (Giancoli Fig. 9-23)

Board sketch: the COM at x_c between the masses; the red arrow x_c - x_1 from m_1 to the COM, the green arrow x_2 - x_c from the COM to m_2; below, x_1, x_c and x_2, all measured from x = 0.

The balance condition. Each weight tries to turn the beam about the finger, the left one anticlockwise, the right one clockwise. By the lever rule (school "Hebelgesetz"), the turning effect of a force is force × lever arm, and the beam stays level only if the two turning effects are equal:

(x_c - x_1) \cdot m_1 \cdot g = (x_2 - x_c) \cdot m_2 \cdot g
Symbols
  • x_1, x_2 — positions of mass 1 and mass 2, measured from x = 0 (m)
  • x_c — position of the center of mass (m); index c for "center"
  • x_c - x_1, x_2 - x_c — the lever arms: distance of each mass from the COM (m), both positive for x_1 < x_c < x_2
  • m_1 g, m_2 g — the two weights (N)

The proper name for "turning effect" is torque (10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy); here only the balance matters. The board crosses out g on both sides: it is a common factor, so the COM depends only on masses and positions, not on gravity.

Solving for x_c (p. 4–5; the board circles the two x_c terms green, the ones to collect):

\begin{aligned} (x_c - x_1)\,m_1 &= (x_2 - x_c)\,m_2 && \text{(divide both sides by } g \neq 0) \\ x_c m_1 - x_1 m_1 &= x_2 m_2 - x_c m_2 && \text{(multiply out both brackets)} \\ x_c m_1 + x_c m_2 &= x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2 && \text{(add } x_c m_2 + x_1 m_1 \text{ to both sides)} \\ x_c\,(m_1 + m_2) &= x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2 && \text{(factor out } x_c) \\ x_c &= \frac{x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} && \text{(divide by } m_1 + m_2 > 0) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. The boxed result on the board is the last line. It confirms the first expectation: with m_2 > m_1, the position x_2 gets the larger weight, so x_c moves towards m_2. Two limiting cases: with m_1 = 0 the formula gives x_c = x_2, the COM sits on the only mass; and if x_1 = x_2, x_c is that common point.

Giancoli takes this formula as the definition of the center of mass, x_c = (m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2)/M with the total mass M = m_1 + m_2, and shows later that with this definition the point moves as described in section 6. The lecture's lever balance arrives at the same formula and shows why it is the balance point.

If m_1 = m_2 (board): replace m_2 by m_1, factor m_1 out of the numerator and cancel it (crossed out on the board):

x_c = \frac{x_1 \cdot m_1 + x_2 \cdot m_1}{2 m_1} = \frac{m_1\,(x_1 + x_2)}{2 m_1} = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}

Symbols as above. The ordinary average of the two positions, the midpoint, as expected.

Intuition

The center of mass is a mass-weighted average of the positions: each position counts as often as its mass. Heavier masses pull the average towards themselves. A seesaw with a heavy child near the pivot and a light child far out balances for the same reason.

3 Many masses: discrete notation

Lecture: board p. 5 · Giancoli §9-8

With more masses on the beam the board simply appends terms in red:

x_c = \frac{x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2 + x_3 m_3 + x_4 m_4 + \ldots}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3 + m_4 + \ldots}
Symbols
  • m_3, m_4, \ldots — further masses (kg) at the positions x_3, x_4, \ldots (m); other symbols as above

Why appending is allowed: write the two-mass balance with everything on one side, m_1(x_1 - x_c) + m_2(x_2 - x_c) = 0. Here the left mass has a negative lever arm, the right one a positive arm, and the turning effects cancel. Every further mass adds its own term of the same shape:

\begin{aligned} m_1(x_1 - x_c) + m_2(x_2 - x_c) + m_3(x_3 - x_c) + \ldots &= 0 && \text{(all turning effects cancel)} \\ (x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2 + x_3 m_3 + \ldots) - x_c\,(m_1 + m_2 + m_3 + \ldots) &= 0 && \text{(multiply out, collect the } x_c \text{ terms)} \\ x_c &= \frac{x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2 + x_3 m_3 + \ldots}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3 + \ldots} && \text{(solve for } x_c) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above.

With the sum sign this is the board's discrete notation ("→ more masses"), and the same formula holds for the other two coordinates:

x_c = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \cdot m_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i}, \qquad y_c = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i \cdot m_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i}, \qquad z_c = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i \cdot m_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i}
Symbols
  • n — number of masses; i — index running over them, i = 1, 2, \ldots, n
  • m_i — mass of the i-th body (kg); x_i, y_i, z_i — its coordinates (m)
  • \sum_{i=1}^{n} — "add up the following for i = 1 to n"; the denominator \sum_i m_i is the total mass M
  • x_c, y_c, z_c — coordinates of the center of mass (m)

The board writes "i = n" on top of each \sum and just "i" underneath; it means the usual "from i = 1 to n". For n = 3: \sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i m_i = x_1 m_1 + x_2 m_2 + x_3 m_3. Discrete means a countable number of separate masses, as opposed to the continuous body in section 4.

Why the same formula works for y and z: nothing in the derivation used that the beam lies along x. Balancing the body about a line parallel to the y-axis gives x_c, about a line parallel to the x-axis gives y_c, and so on. Each coordinate is averaged on its own, always with the same weights m_i. Together they form the position vector of the COM, which the three formulas combine into one vector equation:

\vec r_c = \begin{pmatrix} x_c \\ y_c \\ z_c \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i\,\vec r_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i} = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i\,\vec r_i
Symbols
  • \vec r_c — position vector of the center of mass (m); \vec r_i = (x_i, y_i, z_i)^\top — position vector of mass i (m)
  • M = \sum_i m_i — total mass (kg)

The coordinates of the COM depend on where the origin is; the physical point does not. Moving the origin shifts all x_i and x_c by the same amount.

Common mistake — forgetting the weights or the denominator

Two tempting shortcuts: averaging the positions without the masses (\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2} is only right for equal masses), or adding the x_i m_i and forgetting to divide by the total mass. In the second case the result has the unit kg·m, not m, a free check. Also measure every position from the same origin.

Worked example — COM of three masses in a plane

A small robot platform carries a battery of 2\,\mathrm{kg} at (2\,\mathrm{m}, 0), and two motors of 1\,\mathrm{kg} each at (0, 0) and (0, 4\,\mathrm{m}).

  1. Total mass: M = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4\,\mathrm{kg}.
  2. x-coordinate (weighted average): x_c = \dfrac{1 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 0}{4}\,\mathrm{m} = 1\,\mathrm{m}.
  3. y-coordinate, same weights: y_c = \dfrac{1 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 4}{4}\,\mathrm{m} = 1\,\mathrm{m}.
  4. Check: the COM (1\,\mathrm{m}, 1\,\mathrm{m}) lies inside the triangle of the three masses ✓, and closer to the heavy battery than the plain average of the corners, (0.67\,\mathrm m, 1.33\,\mathrm m) ✓.

4 Extended bodies: continuous notation

Lecture: board p. 5 (bottom) – p. 6 (top) · Giancoli §9-8

Board sketch (p. 5): a potato-shaped body, cut into many small slices along its lower edge; single pieces are labelled m_{37}, m_{38} and, far away, m_{9873}. A red rectangle is drawn around it with its two diagonals crossing in a red point. Your notes: "What if arbitrary mass?"

A real body is not a few separate masses but a lump of material. The labels m_{37}, m_{38}, m_{9873} say: cut it into thousands of small pieces and number them; then the discrete formula still applies, with a huge n. The red rectangle with crossing diagonals marks the middle of the potato's outline, and that point is generally not the COM: if the potato is fatter on one side, more pieces sit there and pull the weighted average towards them. The COM can't be read off the outline; the pieces have to be added up.

From the sum to the integral. Make the pieces smaller and more numerous. In the limit each piece is an infinitesimally small mass \mathrm dm at a position x, and "add up over all pieces" becomes an integral, the same move as in 4.1 Integral Calculus, where a sum of thin strips became an area:

The sum becomes an integral: cut the body into tiny pieces \Delta m_i, each at its position \vec r_i; as the pieces shrink, \Delta m_i \to \mathrm dm. (Giancoli Fig. 9-26)

For a thin rod the piece is a short slice of length \mathrm dx at position x, with mass \mathrm dm = \lambda\,\mathrm dx (\lambda = mass per length). This is the set-up of Exercise Set 0, Problem 10. (Giancoli Fig. 9-27)

\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\,m_i \;\longrightarrow\; \int_m x\,\mathrm dm, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \;\longrightarrow\; \int_m \mathrm dm
Symbols
  • \mathrm dm — mass of one tiny piece of the body (kg); x — that piece's position (m)
  • \int_m — "integrate over all the mass of the body"

This gives the board's continuous notation ("→ continuous notation"):

x_c = \frac{\int_m x\,\mathrm{d}m}{\int_m \mathrm{d}m}
Symbols
  • \mathrm{d}m — mass of a tiny piece (kg); x — its position (m)
  • \int_m \mathrm{d}m = m — the total mass (kg)
  • x_c — x-coordinate of the center of mass (m); y_c, z_c the same way with y, z

Density. Integrating "over the mass" is awkward, because a body is described by where it is, its volume. The density converts one into the other:

\rho = \frac{m}{V} \ \ \text{(homogeneous body)}, \qquad \mathrm dm = \rho\,\mathrm dV
Symbols
  • \rho — density: mass per volume (kg/m³)
  • m — mass (kg); V — volume of the body (m³); \mathrm{d}V — volume of a tiny piece (m³)

The board writes: "\rho = \text{const.}; \rho(x, y, z) \Rightarrow \text{CONST.}" and "m = V \cdot \rho, \mathrm{d}m = \mathrm{d}V\,\rho — only works if density is const." Read it as: in general the density may change from point to point, \rho(x, y, z), but from now on we assume it is the same everywhere. The relation \mathrm dm = \rho\,\mathrm dV for a small piece is always true with the local density; m = V\rho and pulling \rho out of the integral need a constant \rho.

With a constant \rho, substitute in numerator and denominator:

\begin{aligned} \int_m x\,\mathrm dm &= \int_V x\,\rho\,\mathrm dV = \rho\int_V x\,\mathrm dV && \text{(replace } \mathrm dm\text{; constant } \rho \text{ comes out)} \\ \int_m \mathrm dm &= \rho\int_V \mathrm dV = \rho\,V = m && \text{(same for the denominator)} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • \int_V — integral over the whole volume of the body; other symbols as above

So, as on the board (the \rho's crossed out, the denominator bracketed red "= m"):

x_c = \frac{\rho \int_V x\,\mathrm{d}V}{\rho \int_V \mathrm{d}V} = \frac{\int_V x\,\mathrm{d}V}{\int_V \mathrm{d}V}, \qquad y_c = \frac{\rho \int_V y\,\mathrm{d}V}{\rho \int_V \mathrm{d}V} = \frac{\int_V y\,\mathrm{d}V}{\int_V \mathrm{d}V}

Symbols as above.

What does it mean that \rho cancels?

For a body of uniform material, the center of mass depends only on its shape, not on what it is made of: a steel cube and a wooden cube of the same size have their COM in the same place, the geometric center (centroid). That is only true for constant density. A hammer (heavy steel head, light wooden handle) has its COM near the head, not in the middle of its outline; there \rho(x, y, z) would have to stay inside the integrals.

5 Example: the cuboid, and symmetry

Lecture: board p. 6 – p. 8 (top) · Giancoli §9-8

Board sketch (p. 6): left, the axes (z up, y into the page, x to the right); middle, a cuboid whose edges run from x_1 to x_2, y_1 to y_2, z_1 to z_2, with a small box \mathrm dV drawn inside; right, a sketch of the cuboid's corner at the axes.

A homogeneous cuboid occupies the points with

x_1 \le x \le x_2, \qquad y_1 \le y \le y_2, \qquad z_1 \le z \le z_2
Symbols
  • x_1, x_2; y_1, y_2; z_1, z_2 — the cuboid's lower and upper bounds along each axis (m)

A point belongs to the cuboid exactly when all three hold, so these are the limits of integration. Plan: compute the mass (the denominator) first, then the numerator \int_V x\,\mathrm dV, then divide.

Mass. Cut the cuboid into tiny boxes \mathrm dx wide, \mathrm dy deep and \mathrm dz high, so \mathrm dV = \mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dz, and add them all up with a triple integral, one direction at a time:

m_\text{cuboid} = \rho \int_V \mathrm{d}V = \rho \iiint_{x\,y\,z} \mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z
Symbols
  • m_\text{cuboid} — mass of the cuboid (kg); \rho — its constant density (kg/m³)
  • \mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z — a tiny box of volume \mathrm dV
  • \iiint — a triple integral: one integral for each of x, y, z

The board writes the limits on and integrates the constant 1, z first:

\begin{aligned} m_\text{cuboid} &= \rho \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\int_{y_1}^{y_2}\!\int_{z_1}^{z_2} 1 \,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x && \text{(innermost integral belongs to } \mathrm dz) \\ &= \rho \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\int_{y_1}^{y_2} z\Big|_{z_1}^{z_2} \,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x && \text{(antiderivative of 1 in } z \text{ is } z) \\ &= \rho \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\int_{y_1}^{y_2} (z_2 - z_1)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x && \text{(upper minus lower limit)} \\ &= \rho \cdot (z_2 - z_1) \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\int_{y_1}^{y_2} 1 \,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x && \text{(the height is a constant for } y, x) \\ &= \rho \cdot \underbrace{(z_2 - z_1) \cdot (y_2 - y_1) \cdot (x_2 - x_1)}_{V} && \text{(the same twice more)} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • z\big|_{z_1}^{z_2} — "evaluate at the upper limit minus at the lower limit", = z_2 - z_1
  • V — the cuboid's volume (m³), bracketed red on the board; other symbols as above

For a cuboid any order of integration works, because all the limits are constants. Height × depth × width is the volume, so m_\text{cuboid} = \rho V, as it must be. The board then writes m_\text{cuboid} = \rho \cdot x\,y\,z with x \to WIDTH, y \to LENGTH, z \to HEIGHT.

Common mistake — overloaded letters

In "m_\text{cuboid} = \rho\,x\,y\,z" the letters are not coordinates any more; they stand for the side lengths x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1, z_2 - z_1. Inside the integrals, x, y, z are still coordinates. Don't insert a coordinate where a side length is meant.

Integrating a constant (side note on p. 7, "such as: C" a constant), written without "+\,\text{const.}", which cancels in definite integrals anyway:

\int C \,\mathrm{d}x = C \cdot x, \qquad \int C x \,\mathrm{d}x = C\,\frac{x^2}{2}, \qquad \int C\,\frac{x^2}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x = C\,\frac{x^3}{3 \cdot 2}
Symbols
  • C — any constant (it can be pulled out of the integral); x — integration variable

All three are the power rule \int x^n\,\mathrm dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} (n \neq -1) for n = 0, 1, 2, with C carried along. Check the last one by differentiating back: \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\,C\frac{x^3}{6} = C\frac{x^2}{2} ✓. The first line was used for the mass; the second is needed now.

Center of mass. For x_c = \int_V x\,\mathrm{d}V \big/ \int_V \mathrm{d}V the board boxes the numerator green "→ OPEN" and the denominator red "→ ✓": the denominator is already known, V. The numerator, with every step:

\begin{aligned} \int_V x\,\mathrm{d}V &= \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\int_{y_1}^{y_2}\!\int_{z_1}^{z_2} x \,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x && \text{(limits as before)} \\ &= \int_{x_1}^{x_2}\!\int_{y_1}^{y_2} x\,(z_2 - z_1)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x && (x \text{ is constant while only } z \text{ changes)} \\ &= \int_{x_1}^{x_2} x\,(z_2 - z_1)(y_2 - y_1)\,\mathrm{d}x && \text{(no } y \text{ in it either)} \\ &= (z_2 - z_1)(y_2 - y_1)\int_{x_1}^{x_2} x \,\mathrm{d}x && \text{(pull the constants out)} \\ &= (z_2 - z_1)(y_2 - y_1)\cdot\frac{x^2}{2}\Big|_{x_1}^{x_2} = \frac{(z_2 - z_1)\,(y_2 - y_1)\,(x_2^2 - x_1^2)}{2} && \text{(power rule, insert the limits)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. (The board skips the second and third lines and writes "″" for "same as the line above".) Dividing numerator (green) by denominator (red):

\begin{aligned} x_c &= \frac{(z_2 - z_1)\,(y_2 - y_1)\,(x_2^2 - x_1^2)}{2\,(z_2 - z_1)\,(y_2 - y_1)\,(x_2 - x_1)} && \text{(numerator over } V) \\ &= \frac{x_2^2 - x_1^2}{2\,(x_2 - x_1)} && \text{(cancel height and depth, both} \neq 0) \\ &= \frac{(x_2 - x_1)\,(x_2 + x_1)}{2\,(x_2 - x_1)} && (p^2 - q^2 = (p - q)(p + q)) \\ &= \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2} && \text{(cancel } x_2 - x_1 \neq 0) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • x_c — x-coordinate of the cuboid's center of mass (m); other symbols as above

The boxed result: the middle of the cuboid in x. The same calculation with y or z gives y_c = \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2} and z_c = \frac{z_1 + z_2}{2}, so the COM is the cuboid's center.

Intuition

Symmetry decides before you integrate. A homogeneous body that looks the same on both sides of a plane must balance on that plane, so its COM lies on every plane of symmetry. For a cuboid, sphere or cylinder the COM is the geometric center; the integral above just confirms what symmetry predicts. The integral is needed for shapes without enough symmetry.

Worked example — a shape without symmetry: a triangular plate

A thin homogeneous triangular plate has corners (0, 0), (b, 0) and (0, h). Find its COM. (Thin and homogeneous: use areas instead of volumes, x_c = \int_A x\,\mathrm dA / A, by the same cancelling of \rho and the thickness.)

  1. Describe the shape by limits. For a given x between 0 and b, the plate reaches from y = 0 up to the slanted edge y = h\,(1 - x/b).
  2. Area (denominator): A = \int_0^b\!\int_0^{h(1 - x/b)} 1\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx = \int_0^b h\,(1 - \tfrac{x}{b})\,\mathrm dx = h\,(b - \tfrac{b}{2}) = \tfrac12 b h ✓ (the triangle formula).
  3. Numerator: \int_0^b\!\int_0^{h(1 - x/b)} x\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx = \int_0^b x\,h\,(1 - \tfrac{x}{b})\,\mathrm dx = h\left(\tfrac{b^2}{2} - \tfrac{b^2}{3}\right) = \tfrac{1}{6}\,b^2 h.
  4. Divide: x_c = \dfrac{b^2 h/6}{b h/2} = \dfrac{b}{3}. In the same way y_c = \dfrac{h}{3}.
  5. Read it: the COM sits a third of the way in from the right-angle corner, not in the middle (b/2): more of the plate lies near the tall side. A plate with b = 0.6\,\mathrm m, h = 0.3\,\mathrm m balances at (0.2\,\mathrm m,\ 0.1\,\mathrm m).
Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §9-8, §9-9)
  • Composite bodies: a body made of simple parts (an L-shaped plate, a robot arm of links) is handled by finding each part's mass and COM (by symmetry), then treating the parts as point masses in the discrete formula. The COM can lie outside the material, e.g. in the hole of a ring.
  • Finding it by experiment: hang the body from one point, draw the vertical line through the suspension point, repeat from a second point; the COM is where the lines cross, because a hanging body comes to rest with its COM straight below the suspension.

Symmetry and splitting into parts together: an L-shaped plate is two rectangles A and B, each with its COM in its middle. The COM of the whole L lies between them, here outside the material. The COM is a point in space, not necessarily a point of the body. (Giancoli Fig. 9-29)

Problem-solving steps — finding a center of mass
  1. Choose axes and an origin; use symmetry: the COM lies on every symmetry plane, so those coordinates are known without calculation.
  2. Point masses: list m_i and the coordinates; x_c = \sum x_i m_i / \sum m_i, the same for y and z.
  3. Solid body with constant density: describe the body by integration limits, compute V = \int_V \mathrm dV, then \int_V x\,\mathrm dV, and divide.
  4. Composite body: find the COM and mass of each simple part (by symmetry), then treat the parts as point masses.
  5. Check: the unit is a length; the COM lies towards the heavier side; it agrees with any symmetry.

6 The mass point model

Lecture: board p. 8 · Giancoli §9-9

Board sketch (p. 8): the car, an arrow, and a single small point labelled "MASS POINT".

Once the COM is known, a body can be modelled as a mass point (point mass): all of its mass concentrated in that one point, with no size and no orientation. This is the standard simplification whenever the body's size and rotation don't matter for the question, such as "where is the car after 2 s?". From 4 Kinematics – Position, Velocity and Acceleration on, a car, a stone or a robot is a point that moves, and its position is the position of its COM.

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §9-9)

The book proves why the model works: differentiating M\vec r_c = \sum m_i\vec r_i twice and using Newton's laws (8 Newton's Laws and Forces), the internal forces between the parts cancel in pairs (reaction principle), and what remains is

M\,\vec a_c = \sum\vec F_\text{ext}

The COM moves like a single particle of mass M on which all external forces act. Its velocity gives the total momentum, M\vec v_c = \sum m_i\vec v_i, which is why momentum is conserved when no external force acts (12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions › 7 Conservation of momentum).

A rocket breaks into two equal halves at the top of its path: the pieces fly apart, but their common center of mass continues on the original parabola, because the explosion's forces are internal. (Giancoli Fig. 9-32)

  • M — total mass (kg); \vec a_c, \vec v_c — acceleration and velocity of the COM; \sum\vec F_\text{ext} — sum of the forces from outside the body (N)
Connection

The center of mass returns in Introduction to Robotics: a wheeled robot doesn't tip as long as its center of gravity lies inside the triangle of its wheels (1 Introduction › Number of wheels).
